In addition to non-pharmacological strategies and a causal treatment, a pharmacological therapy may be necessary to control the symptoms. Alpha-2-agonists are available for stress-reduction and treatment of vegetative symptoms, and benzodiazepines can be used for anxiolysis (Table 14 ). Pharmacological therapy of delirium Preventive measures for delirium are both safe and effective [ ]. If delirium does occur, it should be treated promptly and symptomatically. The treatment of psychotic symptoms (with or without delirium) may include low-dose neuroleptics [ ]. In addition, the use of alpha-2 agonists is also suitable for a symptom-orientated therapy of delirium [ ], [ ]. A special situation is the alcohol withdrawal delirium in the ICU, for which long-acting benzodiazepines should be considered [ ] (Table 15 ). Weaning from mechanical ventilation The new German S2k-Guidelines on “Prolonged Weaning” AWMF (020/015) provides recommendations regarding weaning from mechanical ventilation [ ]. The management of analgesia, sedation, and delirium influence the weaning process significantly [ ]. In order to start weaning as early as possible, it is useful to combine sedation and weaning protocols (Table 16 ). Treatment with neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBA) There is no indication for a general use of a neuromuscular blockade during intensive care treatment. During neuromuscular blockade, patients cannot be awake, actively participate in their recovery, nor benefit from physiotherapy. When there is a specific indication for NMBAs, adequate analgesia and sedation should be provided [ ]. Furthermore, the depth of blockade should be monitored [ ], and the duration should be kept as short as possible (Table 17 ). Intra- and inter- hospital transports Especially during intra- and inter-hospital transports, movements or changes in the position of the patient are potentially painful events. Therefore, a symptomatic therapy should be continued and possibly adjusted during a transport [ ]. An inadequate sedation (over- and under-sedation) should be avoided at all times, as this can lead to an acute deterioration of neurological and cardiovascular parameters (Table 18 ). Analgesia, sedation, and delirium management in special patients Pregnant and breastfeeding women in the ICU The pharmacotherapy of pregnant and breastfeeding patients in the ICU is particularly challenging, as it must account for the effects of the drugs on the unborn or breast-fed child. Due to the lack of randomized-controlled trials, there is little evidence for pharmacotherapy of pregnant or breastfeeding women. Should there be an indication for opioids or sedatives during these periods, an adequate monitoring of the child is obligatory (Table 19 ). End-of-life care Impending death is a period that can be severely influenced by anxiety, stress, and pain. Dying patients require the same patient-centred care as other ICU patients. Frequent monitoring and sufficient pharmacotherapy should ensure the patient is free of discomfort, even if this leads to a acceleration of the dying process [ ]. This guideline should be used and evaluated in the light and in-line with the “guideline of limitations to intensive care treatment” [ ] and the “basic principles for medical palliative care”, published by the German Medical Association [ ] (Table 20 ). Patients with severe burn injury Severe burn injuries lead to strong pain, possible hyperalgesia, as well as a prolonged hospitalization. Aside from an adequate basic level of analgesia, additional analgesics (local and systemic) and/or procedural sedation may be necessary when performing various procedures (e.g. dressing changes). There are multimodal concepts for the use of analgesics, adjuvants, and non-pharmacological strategies regarding pain management in patients with severe burns [ ]. Especially for analgesia and sedation of burn-injured children, the use of standardized protocols and training programs should be used [ ] (Table 21 , Table 22 ). Multiple trauma patients The German AWMF-guideline registered under 012/019 provides recommendations regarding patients with multiple trauma [ ]. There is no evidence for a clear superiority of a particular drug for analgesia in severely injured patients. Opioids (morphine, fentanyl, sufentanil, alfentanil, remifentanil), ketamine [ ] (s-enantiomer, racemate), and adjuvant alpha-2-agonists (clonidine) are used routinely in the clinic. Due to an increased risk for adrenal insufficiency and numerous alternatives, etomidate should no longer be used for procedural sedation, and is no longer recommended in trauma patients. Nevertheless, there is no evidence that the administration of etomidate has long-term effects on outcome [ ], [ ] (Table 23 ). Patients with intracranial hypertension A main focus of the intensive care management of patients with severe traumatic brain injury is the reduction of secondary damage. Although there is little evidence that sedation directly lowers intra-cranial-pressure (ICP), the acute treatment of patients with elevated ICP starts with a deep sedation (RASS-5). There are no validated monitoring systems for this patient subgroup, so the general scores and monitoring instruments are used [ ]. A frequent neurological examination

in trauma patients. Nevertheless, there is no evidence that the administration of etomidate has long-term effects on outcome [ ], [ ] (Table 23 ). Patients with intracranial hypertension A main focus of the intensive care management of patients with severe traumatic brain injury is the reduction of secondary damage. Although there is little evidence that sedation directly lowers intra-cranial-pressure (ICP), the acute treatment of patients with elevated ICP starts with a deep sedation (RASS-5). There are no validated monitoring systems for this patient subgroup, so the general scores and monitoring instruments are used [ ]. A frequent neurological examination is obligatory. The choice of sedatives should be in-line with recommendations made in the general part. An ideal analgesic/sedative for patients with elevated intracranial pressure should decrease ICP while sustaining an adequate cerebral perfusion pressure, as well as maintain cerebral hemodynamics, including cerebral autoregulation. Additionally, it should reduce the cerebral metabolic rate for oxygen (CMRO2), have anticonvulsive and neuroprotective properties, and should allow short wake-up times for the assessment of patients after a brief infusion interruption [ ] (Table 24 ). Cardiac surgery Fast-track concepts include a 2-hour sedation phase after uncomplicated cardiac surgery. In this setting, numerous analgesia and sedation protocols have proven to be advantageous [ ], and fast-track strategies seem to reduce the incidence of postoperative delirium [ ]. Delirium in cardiac surgical patients is associated with a higher mortality [ ], so that a delirium screening with a validated tool – as generally recommended – is especially important [ ], [ ] (Table 25 ). Patients on extracorporeal life support systems (ECLS) There is a grey area regarding the level of sedation for patients on ECLS, where safety-aspects and the ability to positively influence recovery must be balanced. Patients on ECLS have numerous delirium risk-factors. Hyperactive delirium or agitation can be life-threatening for these patients, so that a consequent monitoring and a symptomatic therapy of stress, anxiety, delirium, pain, and insomnia is essential to safely achieve a target RASS of 0 [ ], [ ], [ ], [ ], [ ] (Table 26 ). Special positioning of patients Positioning therapy is used for prophylaxis and treatment of respiratory dysfunctions [ ], and requires an individual sedation target. Changes of the position frequently represent a challenge for the symptomatic treatment of anxiety, stress, and pain. Therefore, a symptom-orientated therapy should be adapted for changing demands during positioning therapy. Though a deep sedation may be indicated for patient repositioning, [ ], [ ], an excessive sedation should be avoided. Analgesia, sedation, and delirium management in children Monitoring For the monitoring of analgesia, sedation, and delirium in children, there are validated monitoring scales are that take developmental stage into account [ ]. Also in the pediatric intensive care, adequate monitoring and individual therapy goals are essential for successful patient-oriented care (Table 27 , Table 28 , Table 29 ). Generally, children aged ≥3 years are able to evaluate pain-levels. Even in children, a self-assessment of pain is superior to observational scales [ ], and the Faces Pain Scale-revised has been well-established as a valid monitoring tool [ ]. If children are unable to assess their pain, there are several age-appropriate observational pain assessment scales. However, both in very premature infants as well as in children and adolescents with neurocognitive impairment, those instruments have a limited value and tend to systematically underestimate pain [ ], [ ], [ ]. Combined pain and distress sedation scales have been validated for the monitoring of sedation in children. For premature and full-term neonates, the Neonatal Pain, Agitation and Sedation Scale (N-PASS) is available. For infants and toddlers, the COMFORTneo Scale and the Comfort-B Scale are available. Additionally, there are special scales for assessing opioid or sedative withdrawal following a continuous therapy. Children can also suffer from delirium, and their symptoms are often misinterpreted. The pediatric critical care community has a need for a systematic delirium screening with validated tools [ ], [ ], [ ], [ ]. Treatment strategies in children Critically ill children – like adults – require an individual pain therapy adapted to their current situation. This includes multimodal therapy strategies for opioids, non-opioids, and regional analgesia, as well as for local anesthetics, co-analgesics and non-pharmacological procedures (Table 30 , Table 31 , Table 32 , Table 33 ). When regarding analgesia in children, it is important to consider that pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics differ with age. Additional and supportive procedures for analgesia are also recommended for children. There are different non-pharmacological procedures available that can be used for co-analgesia, per example the administration of oral glucose, non-nutritive suction for neonates, or virtual reality for pediatric burn patients. Children require sedation, sometimes continuously, in order to undergo certain diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. For sedation in children, special personnel and structural prerequisites are

local anesthetics, co-analgesics and non-pharmacological procedures (Table 30 , Table 31 , Table 32 , Table 33 ). When regarding analgesia in children, it is important to consider that pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics differ with age. Additional and supportive procedures for analgesia are also recommended for children. There are different non-pharmacological procedures available that can be used for co-analgesia, per example the administration of oral glucose, non-nutritive suction for neonates, or virtual reality for pediatric burn patients. Children require sedation, sometimes continuously, in order to undergo certain diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. For sedation in children, special personnel and structural prerequisites are required. Oversedation should be avoided as always, and careful titration is required to keep dosages as low as possible. There is still a high demand for research regarding pediatric delirium. In principle, it is essential to detect delirious symptoms as early as possible and identify and neutralize potential causes. Current evidence revealed a combination of psychological, social (presence of family, toys, pictures of home, normal day-night rhythm, etc.), and pharmacological interventions to be effective [ ]. Analgesia, sedation, and delirium management in elderly patients The “clinical age” is determined by the biological age, frailty, comorbidities, long-term medication, and external influences. The ageing of the cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, and nervous-systems lead to changes in pharmacodynamics and kinetics. The inherent age cannot be based on a chronological age alone (Table 34 , Table 35 ). Elderly patients lack the resources to compensate for delirium-associated complications, thus a frequent and active screening for delirium is paramount. In principle, all monitoring instruments used for the adult patients may be used for elderly patients. To evaluate pain in patients with cognitive impairment or dementia, tools such as Faces Pain Scale, PAINAD-scale as well as the BESD-scale (German scale) are available. Preventive measures such as reorientation, visual and hearing aids are especially indicated for elderly patients [ ]. Regarding the treatment of delirium, a symptomatic treatment should consider the delirogenic effects of long-acting benzodiazepines [ ], the cardiac side effects of neuroleptics, and the use of appropriately cautious dosages [ ], [ ], [ ]. For the treatment of delirium, melatonin or melatonin-analogues should be considered at night to reduce the incidence and duration of delirium [ ]. Economy, quality assurance and implementation of the guideline In terms of quality assurance, management of analgesia, sedation and delirium in the ICU should be conducted according to guidelines and subject to a continuous quality verification [ ]. This includes the regular training of personnel in the implementation of the guidelines [ ]. Special consideration for regional characteristics and internal Standard Operating Procedures improved the integration of guideline recommendations [ ]. As a follow-up to the surveys of 2002 and 2006, a current survey on the current implementation of the S3-guideline in clinical routine is being carried out and will be published. Before the next guideline update process, an additional survey will assess the level of implementation (Table 36 ). chunks.content: STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY This study employs a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled design to minimise bias. The use of a fixed 50 µg dose of dexmedetomidine nasal spray enhances dosing accuracy and clinical feasibility. Sleep quality is assessed using both subjective scales (Numerical Rating Scale, Athens Insomnia Scale, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) and objective monitoring with a wearable device. The homogeneous population (patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy) helps control for surgical variability. The study does not utilise polysomnography, which may limit the depth of sleep architecture analysis. Introduction Postsurgical sleep disturbance (PSD) is a frequent and clinically significant complication after surgery, with reported incidence ranging from 15% to 72%. Older patients, women, those experiencing severe postoperative pain and individuals with preoperative anxiety are at particularly high risk. PSD not only compromises patient comfort but also predisposes to postoperative delirium and cognitive dysfunction, ultimately delaying functional recovery and hospital discharge. General anaesthesia itself has been identified in multiple studies as an independent risk factor for PSD. Despite its clinical importance, no standardised preventive strategy has been widely adopted. Dexmedetomidine, a highly selective α₂-adrenergic receptor agonist, produces sedation that closely resembles natural non-rapid eye movement (REM) sleep by activating receptors in the locus coeruleus. It provides both sedative and analgesic effects while maintaining arousability. Low-dose intravenous administration has been shown to improve postoperative sleep quality in intensive care and general ward settings ; however, the requirement for continuous infusion limits its broader application. The intranasal spray formulation of dexmedetomidine offers high bioavailability (83.8%) and convenient administration. Studies in paediatric populations have demonstrated its safety and efficacy as a premedication. Recent adult studies also suggest that a dose of 1–1.5 µg/kg significantly improves postoperative sleep architecture, prolongs N2 and N3 sleep stages, reduces awakenings and lowers Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores. Beyond its direct modulation of sleep architecture, dexmedetomidine’s role in alleviating preoperative negative psychological states is gaining increasing attention. Anxiety and depression are strong predictors of PSD, potentially exacerbating postoperative sleep disruptions by overactivating the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis and the sympathetic nervous system, thereby disturbing circadian rhythms. Dexmedetomidine exerts anxiolytic and antisympathetic effects by centrally inhibiting norepinephrine release. Consequently, we hypothesise that dexmedetomidine may improve PSD through a dual-pathway mechanism: first, by directly simulating physiological sleep, and second, by mitigating pre-existing anxiety/depression, thereby reducing their negative impact on sleep quality at the source. This provides a novel interventional perspective for PSD prevention. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) requires rapid postoperative recovery and early discharge, yet PSD remains common in this population and contributes to unplanned readmission and delayed return to daily activity. There is thus a compelling need for a simple, evidence-based prophylactic strategy. This multicentre, prospective, randomised, double-blind, controlled trial will evaluate whether a fixed 50 µg dose of intranasal dexmedetomidine administered in the evening after LC reduces the incidence of PSD and improves objective sleep architecture. Objective monitoring: Wristwatch-type wearable device (Huawei Watch D2. The medical device registration certificate number for the product is: Guangdong Device Approval 20242071034) will record total sleep time, REM duration, light (N1–N2) and deep (N3) sleep, and number of nocturnal awakenings during the first postoperative night. Subjective evaluation: Validated questionnaires will be administered, including the PSQI for global sleep quality, the Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS) for insomnia symptoms, and the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) for postoperative pain, which may confound sleep outcomes. We hypothesise that compared with placebo, a single 50 µg dose of intranasal dexmedetomidine administered on the evening of surgery will not only improve sleep architecture through its direct sedative effects but may also further reduce the incidence of PSD via the amelioration of preoperative negative emotional states, thereby significantly enhancing both objective and subjective sleep quality while maintaining a favourable safety profile. Method Study objectives Primary Objective: To evaluate the effect of evening administration of dexmedetomidine nasal spray on the incidence of PSD on the first day after LC. Secondary Objectives: To assess the impact of evening dexmedetomidine nasal spray on the quality of recovery and anxiety-depression scores in patients undergoing LC. Study design This study is a multicentre, prospective, randomised, double-blind, controlled trial designed to evaluate the effect of evening dexmedetomidine nasal spray on the incidence of postoperative sleep disturbance in patients undergoing LC. To maintain blinding, the trial medications (dexmedetomidine nasal spray and saline placebo) are identical in appearance. Only the drug administrator will be aware of the group assignments, whereas participants, outcome assessors, and data analysts will remain blinded to the treatment allocation. Participants One day before surgery, the research team will screen patients in strict accordance with the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. If the procedure is scheduled for a Monday, screening will be completed on the preceding Friday. All eligible participants who voluntarily agree to participate will provide written informed consent before formal enrolment ( ). This trial

Only the drug administrator will be aware of the group assignments, whereas participants, outcome assessors, and data analysts will remain blinded to the treatment allocation. Participants One day before surgery, the research team will screen patients in strict accordance with the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. If the procedure is scheduled for a Monday, screening will be completed on the preceding Friday. All eligible participants who voluntarily agree to participate will provide written informed consent before formal enrolment ( ). This trial enrolled patients who met all the following inclusion criteria: (1) aged 18–65 years; (2) scheduled to undergo LC under general anaesthesia; and (3) agreed to participate and provided signed informed consent. Patients were excluded from participation for any of the following reasons: (1) refusal to participate in this study; (2) pre-existing sick sinus syndrome, severe sinus bradycardia (heart rate <50 beats/min), second-degree or higher atrioventricular block without a pacemaker implantation, congenital heart disease accompanied by any arrhythmia or other severe cardiovascular diseases with cardiac function classification ≥class III; (3) preoperative diagnosis of sleep apnoea or Snoring, Tired, Observed apnoea, Pressure, BMI, Age, Neck, Gender (STOP-Bang) score ≥3 with HCO₃⁻≥28 mmol/L; (4) conditions unsuitable for intranasal administration, such as severe rhinitis or nasal deformities; (5) preoperative PSQI score >7; (6) use of sedatives or hypnotic drugs within 1 month prior to surgery; (7) known allergy to dexmedetomidine; (8) body mass index (BMI) >30 kg/m²; (9) severe liver dysfunction (Child-Pugh Class C) or severe renal dysfunction requiring preoperative dialysis; (10) American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status≥IV; (11) inability to comprehend visual analogue scales or presence of language communication barriers; (12) pregnancy or lactation; (13) current participation in other interventional clinical studies; or (14) other conditions deemed by the investigator or supervising physician as unsuitable for study participation. Participants were withdrawn from the study if any of the following occurred: (1) the participant voluntarily requested to withdraw from the study, (2) loss to follow-up, (3) occurrence of a serious adverse event (AE) deemed related to the study intervention, (4) occurrence of a serious postoperative complication that, in the judgement of the investigator or the Ethics Committee, made it inappropriate for the participant to continue in the study (eg, transfer to ICU, delayed discharge), (5) any protocol violation that substantially affected the primary outcome assessment. For all withdrawn participants, the reason for withdrawal was documented in detail. The last available observation or assessment prior to withdrawal was carried forward for the intention-to-treat analysis ( ). Randomisation, allocation concealment and blinding This trial uses a block randomisation method. A random sequence will be generated in SAS V.9.4 or a later version with predefined seed numbers and block lengths, allocating participants to the experimental or control group in a 1:1 ratio. Sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed randomisation cards will then be prepared. These cards will be managed and distributed by authorised personnel who are not involved in participant screening or treatment. After enrolment, the investigator or an authorised staff member will request the allocation from the card administrator. The administrator will retrieve the corresponding card in sequential order, record the participant’s screening number and initials, sign the card and note the unsealing date to complete the allocation process. Both dexmedetomidine and saline solutions are colourless and transparent. Preparation of trial medications is performed by a designated unblinded investigator who is not involved in participant enrolment, anaesthesia administration or postoperative follow-up. The study coordinator will collect the assigned medications based on the allocation results within 1 hour before administration, deliver them to the relevant researchers and record the details in a blinded log. All blinding records will be securely maintained by the principal investigator. Interventions Participants were randomised to either the dexmedetomidine group or the saline control group. Patients assigned to the dexmedetomidine group received intranasal administration (one spray per nostril, 25 µg per spray) between 20:00 and 22:00 on both the evening before surgery and the evening of surgery. The saline control group received an equivalent volume of saline nasal spray at the same time points and in the same manner. The dexmedetomidine nasal spray device used in this study is designed to deliver a fixed, precise dose per spray, ensuring consistent bioavailability and simplifying administration for both healthcare providers and potential future out-of-hospital use. A fixed dose eliminates the complexities and potential errors associated with weight-based calculations in a postoperative ward setting, enhancing clinical utility and patient safety. The study enrolled patients with normal preoperative sleep quality (PSQI<7). For this specific population, our primary goal was to explore the efficacy of a low dose in preventing PSD, thereby prioritising an excellent safety profile. A 50 µg dose represents a conservative yet potentially effective starting point,

used in this study is designed to deliver a fixed, precise dose per spray, ensuring consistent bioavailability and simplifying administration for both healthcare providers and potential future out-of-hospital use. A fixed dose eliminates the complexities and potential errors associated with weight-based calculations in a postoperative ward setting, enhancing clinical utility and patient safety. The study enrolled patients with normal preoperative sleep quality (PSQI<7). For this specific population, our primary goal was to explore the efficacy of a low dose in preventing PSD, thereby prioritising an excellent safety profile. A 50 µg dose represents a conservative yet potentially effective starting point, minimising the risk of haemodynamic side effects, such as bradycardia or hypotension, which are more dose dependent. While intravenous, weight-based intraoperative dosing is common, evidence supports the efficacy of low, fixed-dose intranasal dexmedetomidine in the postoperative period. In summary, the 50 µg fixed dose was chosen to balance proven efficacy from our preliminary data with the highest possible safety, while also aligning with the practical advantages of the nasal spray delivery system. For anaesthesia management, all patients adhered to routine preoperative fasting for 6–8 hours. On entering the operating room, standard monitoring was established, including heart rate, non-invasive blood pressure, pulse oximetry, Bispectral Index (BIS) and nasopharyngeal temperature, with invasive arterial pressure monitoring performed when necessary. Anaesthesia was induced with midazolam (0.015 mg/kg), sufentanil (0.3–0.5 µg/kg) and propofol. Maintenance during surgery was achieved with remifentanil (0.2–0.4 µg/kg/min) and propofol, supplemented with non-depolarising muscle relaxants. Bilateral transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block with 20 mL of 0.375% ropivacaine was performed to enhance analgesia. Prior to induction, dexamethasone (5 mg) was administered to prevent postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). The use of dexmedetomidine, nitrous oxide, scopolamine and penehyclidine was prohibited during anaesthesia. All patients underwent endotracheal intubation for airway management. Intraoperative management targeted a BIS of 40–60, blood pressure fluctuations within 20% of baseline values, and body temperature maintained between 36°C and 37°C. The use of vasoactive drugs was recorded. If intraoperative analgesia was considered insufficient, supplemental sufentanil (5–10 µg/dose) was administered. Before the end of surgery, a 5-HT₃ receptor antagonist and oxycodone could be given to prevent PONV and to provide adjunct analgesia. Routine reversal of neuromuscular blockade was achieved with sugammadex, and all administered medications were meticulously documented. After surgery, patients were transferred to the postanaesthesia care unit (PACU) for extubation, where an anaesthesiologist assessed readiness for PACU discharge. Data collection and management Authorised research personnel (physicians or nurses) thoroughly familiar with the study protocol will conduct patient visits in the surgical ward. These visits will take place in a quiet environment, preferably with the patient’s family members present. The researcher will provide a comprehensive explanation of the study’s purpose, procedures, potential benefits and risks to the patient and/or their legal representative. It will be clearly communicated that postoperative telephone follow-ups will be performed. All questions from the patient and family will be addressed in detail, allowing sufficient time for consideration. Written informed consent will be obtained from the patient and/or their representative only after confirming understanding and voluntary participation. Data will be systematically collected in three main categories: Preoperative baseline data: demographic information (name, gender, date of birth, education level, years of education and BMI), medical history (comorbidities, medication history, smoking and alcohol use, allergies, surgical and anaesthesia history) and disease severity assessments (New York Heart Association (NYHA) cardiac function classification, Charlson Comorbidity Index and ASA physical status limited to classes I–III). Baseline assessments using the QoR-15, MMSE, PSQI, NRS and HADS scales will evaluate quality of recovery, cognitive function, sleep quality, pain and anxiety/depression levels, respectively. Intraoperative monitoring data: details on anaesthetic drug dosages, induction and maintenance protocols, surgical specifics (site, approach and duration), mechanical ventilation parameters (including lowest SpO₂), oxygenation and circulatory metrics (using the average values from the 5 min immediately before induction and the moment of induction as baseline), instances of blood pressure fluctuations >20% from baseline and SpO₂ <90%, usage of vasoactive drugs, fluid balance metrics (blood loss, transfusion details, intake and output) and AEs such as emergence agitation, defined by a Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) score ≥+1. Postoperative follow-up data: assessments will be performed at specific time points—on PACU arrival, the evening of surgery, the morning and evening of postoperative days 1 and 3, and at 30 days postsurgery. Data will include recovery-related AEs (nausea/vomiting, hypoxemia, haemodynamic instability, delirium, etc), blood pressure monitoring results, QoR-15 scores, frequency and severity of nausea/vomiting, resting and movement-evoked pain NRS scores, sleep quality (using AIS, NRS and PSQI), HADS scores, complication rates, hospital readmission rates and tracking until the endpoint event (all-cause mortality). A proprietary medical data platform will be used for multicentre data collection and synchronisation ( https://www.laowaitalk.com/admin/ ). This platform incorporates automated quality checks to minimise errors and ensure high data integrity. Study outcomes Before initiating

Data will include recovery-related AEs (nausea/vomiting, hypoxemia, haemodynamic instability, delirium, etc), blood pressure monitoring results, QoR-15 scores, frequency and severity of nausea/vomiting, resting and movement-evoked pain NRS scores, sleep quality (using AIS, NRS and PSQI), HADS scores, complication rates, hospital readmission rates and tracking until the endpoint event (all-cause mortality). A proprietary medical data platform will be used for multicentre data collection and synchronisation ( https://www.laowaitalk.com/admin/ ). This platform incorporates automated quality checks to minimise errors and ensure high data integrity. Study outcomes Before initiating statistical analysis, the analysis datasets will be clearly defined. This study will use the following datasets: Full analysis set (FAS): subjects determined according to the intention-to-treat principle, comprising all randomised participants who received the study drug at least once. Per-protocol set (PPS): a subset of the FAS that includes all participants who completed the trial without major protocol deviations. Safety set (SS): all participants who received at least one dose of the study treatment and underwent at least one safety assessment; this set will serve as the primary population for safety analyses. Primary outcomes The primary outcome is the incidence of sleep disturbance on the first postoperative day. We defined the occurrence of sleep disturbance on the first postoperative day as an AIS score >6 or a NRS score >6. Analyses will be conducted using the χ 2 test or Fisher’s exact test. The primary analysis will be performed in both the FAS and PPS populations to assess differences in incidence between the trial and control groups. Secondary outcomes Secondary outcomes will be evaluated in the FAS and PPS populations. Statistical comparisons will use appropriate tests based on data type: continuous variables will be analysed with paired t-tests or paired Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for within-group comparisons (pre vs post-treatment) and independent t-tests or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for between-group comparisons; categorical variables will be analysed using the χ 2 test or Fisher’s exact test; and ordinal variables will be assessed using rank-sum tests. Short-term secondary endpoints include Postoperative day 1 quality of recovery. The assessment will be conducted using the QoR-15 scale. Incidence of PONV within 24 hours. PONV within the first 24 hours postoperatively was defined as the occurrence of any of the following criteria: nausea: the patient spontaneously reported feeling ‘nauseated’, ‘sick to the stomach’, or experiencing ‘gastric discomfort’ on regaining consciousness. Vomiting: the active expulsion of gastric contents from the mouth was observed. Retching: involuntary spasmodic contractions of the abdominal and thoracic muscles associated with attempts to vomit were observed, without the expulsion of gastric contents. Severity of nausea within 24 hours after surgery. A NRS will be used, which ranges from 0 to 10 points, with 0 indicating no nausea and 10 indicating the most severe nausea. The number of vomiting episodes within 24 hours after surgery, including retching. Pain scores on postoperative days 1 and 3, assessed using the pain NRS score, including both resting and movement NRS scores. Pain score at postoperative day 30, using telephone follow-up for data collection. Anxiety and depression on postoperative day 1, using HADS score for assessment. Postoperative opioid analgesic consumption, based on electronic inpatient system records. Postoperative hospital length of stay. Incidence of complications within 30 days, based on inpatient diagnosis records. 30-day readmission rate. Postoperative 30-day sleep score, using NRS score, AIS score and PSQI score for assessment. The Huawei Watch D2 will be used to monitor sleep duration, blood pressure and pulse oxygen saturation, monitoring with Huawei Watch D2. Safety outcomes Safety analysis will be based on the SS. The number of occurrences and incidence rates of AEs will be calculated. Between-group comparisons of AE incidence will be performed using the Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. Detailed descriptions of all AEs observed in the trial will be presented in listings. The χ² test will be used to compare the incidence rates of specific AEs—including hypertension, hypotension, bradycardia, hypoxemia, tachycardia and other AEs—between the two groups. Sample size calculation and statistical analysis This study is designed as a superiority trial. Participants in the dexmedetomidine group will receive intranasal dexmedetomidine spray, whereas those in the control group will receive intranasal saline spray. The primary endpoint is the incidence of sleep disturbance. Based on previous literature, it is expected that intranasal dexmedetomidine will reduce the incidence of sleep disturbance on the first postoperative day by 40%. Assuming a power (1-β) of 0.8, a two-sided type I error (α) of 0.05, and a 1:1 allocation ratio, sample size calculations performed using PASS V.15.0 software indicate that at least 117 subjects per group are required. Allowing for an anticipated 10% dropout rate, a minimum of 130 subjects per group—at least 260 participants in total—will be enrolled ( ). An experienced epidemiologist,

receive intranasal saline spray. The primary endpoint is the incidence of sleep disturbance. Based on previous literature, it is expected that intranasal dexmedetomidine will reduce the incidence of sleep disturbance on the first postoperative day by 40%. Assuming a power (1-β) of 0.8, a two-sided type I error (α) of 0.05, and a 1:1 allocation ratio, sample size calculations performed using PASS V.15.0 software indicate that at least 117 subjects per group are required. Allowing for an anticipated 10% dropout rate, a minimum of 130 subjects per group—at least 260 participants in total—will be enrolled ( ). An experienced epidemiologist, skilled in the design, conduct and analysis of clinical trials, will oversee the statistical analysis. This statistician will remain blinded to treatment allocation and will not participate in patient management. The trial will be conducted across multiple clinical centres. Enrolment will be distributed as evenly as feasible to ensure representativeness across sites. Although competitive enrolment will be used, site-specific targets may be adjusted to maintain balance and no single centre will enrol more than 50% of the total sample. Subgroup analyses Predefined subgroup analyses of the primary outcome will be performed according to: Age (<60 vs ≥60 years). Duration of surgery (<2 hour vs ≥2 hour). Duration of anaesthesia (<2 hour vs ≥2 hour). History of hypertension (yes vs no). Preoperative systolic blood pressure (SBP<140 mm Hg vs ≥140 mm Hg). Handling of missing or implausible data Within the FAS, missing primary outcome data (sleep quality NRS and AIS scores at 24 hours postoperatively) will be imputed using the Last Observation Carried Forward method. No imputation will be applied to other missing outcomes. Logical checks will be performed during data management, and any implausible entries will be queried with investigators. Corrections will be made based on written responses before the database is locked. Analyses will be conducted using SAS software (V.9.4 or higher). Descriptive statistics: continuous variables will be summarised with mean, SD, median, IQR, minimum and maximum. Categorical variables will be summarised as frequencies and percentages. Primary efficacy outcome: the incidence of sleep disturbance on postoperative day 1 will be compared between groups using the χ 2 test or Fisher’s exact test. Continuous variables: within-group comparisons (pre vs post-treatment) will use paired t-tests or paired Wilcoxon rank-sum tests; between-group comparisons will use independent t-tests or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Between-group comparisons over time will be analysed using a repeated-measures mixed-effects model. Categorical variables: χ 2 test or Fisher’s exact test. Ordinal variables: rank-sum tests. Safety analysis: AEs will be summarised by number and incidence rate, with between-group comparisons using the χ 2 test or Fisher’s exact test. Unless otherwise specified for the primary outcome, all statistical tests will be two sided, and p <0.05 will be considered statistically significant. Study monitoring An independent monitoring mechanism will be established for this study. Certified monitors will conduct regular on-site and remote audits of all participating research centres to ensure strict adherence to the study protocol and standard operating procedures. Monitoring activities will include, but are not limited to, verifying the compliance of the informed-consent process, the timeliness and accuracy of data recording, the proper implementation of interventions and the reporting and handling of AEs. All data collection and management procedures will comply with Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guidelines and the relevant regulations issued by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) of China, ensuring the scientific integrity of the research process and the authenticity and reliability of the data. A data-safety monitoring plan will be established according to the level of risk associated with the clinical study. All AEs will be documented in detail, appropriately managed and followed until proper resolution or stabilisation of the condition. Serious AEs and unanticipated incidents will be promptly reported to the Ethics Committee, regulatory authorities and the sponsor as required. The principal investigator will conduct regular cumulative reviews of all AEs to evaluate the study’s risk–benefit profile. In double-blind trials, emergency unblinding may be performed when necessary to ensure subject safety and rights. Studies involving more than minimal risk will assign monitors to audit the research data, while high-risk studies will establish an independent Data and Safety Monitoring Board to review cumulative safety and efficacy data and to provide recommendations regarding the continuation of the study. Previous studies have indicated good tolerability for both preoperative medication and sleep improvement in paediatric and adult populations. The dosage selected for this study is 50 µg (approximately equivalent to 0.5–1.5 µg/kg), which falls within a recognised safe and effective range. Dexmedetomidine, a highly selective α₂-adrenergic receptor agonist, demonstrates a favourable safety profile in its nasal-spray formulation, characterised by high bioavailability (83.8%). Previous studies have indicated good tolerability for both preoperative medication and sleep improvement in paediatric and adult populations. The dosage selected for this study is 50 µg (approximately equivalent to 0.5–1.5 µg/kg), which falls within a recognised safe and effective range. Nonetheless, all patients will undergo comprehensive intraoperative and postoperative monitoring of vital signs, including blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation and BIS. An experienced team of anaesthesiologists will be responsible for overall management throughout the process to minimise potential risks such as haemodynamic fluctuations, hypoxemia or excessive sedation. Written informed consent will be obtained from each participant or their legal representative prior to enrolment, after they are fully informed of the study’s purpose, procedures, potential risks and rights. Participants retain the right to withdraw from the study unconditionally at any stage. Data from withdrawn participants will be excluded from the final analysis, and all personally identifiable information will be anonymised during data processing to strictly protect privacy and confidentiality. Collected data will be used solely for the purposes of this research. All electronic and paper records will be stored in locked facilities or encrypted systems with strictly controlled access permissions. Patient and public involvement Patients and the public were not involved in the design, conduct, analysis or reporting of this research. Ethics and dissemination The study has been registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (registration number: ChiCTR2500101205) and is publicly accessible online ( https://www.medicalresearch.org.cn/index ). Any modifications to the study protocol will require further approval from the relevant ethics review committee. The final results of this trial will be submitted for publication in peer-reviewed journals and presented at relevant academic conferences. Discussion This randomised controlled trial aims to investigate the effect of evening administration of dexmedetomidine nasal spray on the incidence of PSD in patients undergoing LC. Its significance lies in providing a feasible, non-invasive preventive strategy to improve postoperative sleep quality and overall recovery. With the widespread adoption of laparoscopic techniques, LC has become a common procedure, underscoring the importance of rapid recovery and early safe discharge. PSD, however, exhibits a high incidence rate (15%–72%) and is closely associated with delirium, cognitive decline, exacerbated pain and delayed recovery, while effective preventive measures remain lacking. Dexmedetomidine, a highly selective α₂-adrenergic receptor agonist, offers multiple benefits, including the induction of a near-physiological sleep state, anxiolysis and analgesia. Notably, its mechanism for improving postoperative sleep may extend beyond direct modulation of sleep centres to include intervention in preoperative negative emotional states, such as anxiety and depression. Preoperative anxiety and depression are independent risk factors for PSD, potentially exacerbating sleep disturbances through disruption of the stress axis and circadian rhythms. By centrally inhibiting norepinephrine release, dexmedetomidine produces significant anxiolytic and sedative effects. Consequently, we hypothesise that dexmedetomidine may act via a dual-pathway mechanism targeting both ‘emotion and sleep’: directly simulating natural sleep and optimising sleep architecture, while concurrently alleviating pre-existing preoperative anxiety/depression to mitigate their negative impact on postoperative sleep, thereby potentially preventing PSD more effectively. The intranasal spray formulation enhances administration convenience and patient compliance. Utilising a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled design, this study systematically evaluates the preventive efficacy of this intervention against PSD. Should this study demonstrate that evening dexmedetomidine nasal spray significantly reduces the incidence of PSD, it would hold substantial clinical translational value. The implications extend beyond offering a novel strategy for managing sleep disorders to optimising the overall perioperative management pathway for surgical patients. The non-invasive intranasal route eliminates the dependency on infusion pumps required for intravenous administration, rendering it particularly suitable for general wards and potentially aligning with trends towards early discharge and home-based recovery. Furthermore, concomitant with sleep improvement, dexmedetomidine’s synergistic anxiolytic and analgesic properties may promote multidimensional postoperative recovery, aligning closely with the core principles of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery protocols, which emphasise comprehensive physiological and psychological recuperation. Although dexmedetomidine has shown potential for improving sleep quality in ICU and general ward settings, high-level evidence regarding its intranasal formulation for PSD prevention remains scarce. This study features a rigorous design, employing standardised assessment tools such as the PSQI, AIS and NRS for multidimensional sleep evaluation. Incorporating secondary endpoints including the QoR-15 scale, HADS and pain scores allows for a comprehensive assessment of the intervention’s impact on recovery quality and psychological state. The specific inclusion of HADS aims to directly test the hypothesis that improvement in emotional state indirectly facilitates sleep. Objective sleep architecture recording via wearable devices further enhances the reliability and persuasiveness of the findings. This study also has several limitations. First, while the multicentre design improves the generalisability of results, consistency in protocol implementation across different centres requires attention. Second, although

tools such as the PSQI, AIS and NRS for multidimensional sleep evaluation. Incorporating secondary endpoints including the QoR-15 scale, HADS and pain scores allows for a comprehensive assessment of the intervention’s impact on recovery quality and psychological state. The specific inclusion of HADS aims to directly test the hypothesis that improvement in emotional state indirectly facilitates sleep. Objective sleep architecture recording via wearable devices further enhances the reliability and persuasiveness of the findings. This study also has several limitations. First, while the multicentre design improves the generalisability of results, consistency in protocol implementation across different centres requires attention. Second, although subjective sleep assessments are supplemented by objective monitoring, future research could incorporate more precise methods like polysomnography (PSG) for deeper analysis of sleep architecture changes. The follow-up period primarily focuses on the first 30 postoperative days; longer term sleep quality changes warrant further investigation. Finally, although we assessed changes in anxiety and depression scores (HADS), mediation analysis exploring their relationship with sleep improvement might be limited by the study design. Future studies could incorporate more frequent assessment timepoints to elucidate the causal pathway better. Strengths and limitations Strengths This study offers several methodological and practical strengths. The multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled design minimises implementation and measurement biases, generating high-level evidence for evaluating the preventive effect of intranasal dexmedetomidine on PSD. The intervention—evening nasal spray administration—is highly feasible and promotes patient adherence, avoiding the need for specialised equipment or continuous monitoring associated with intravenous infusion, making it particularly suitable for day-surgery and general-ward settings. The protocol does not impose excessive restrictions on intraoperative anaesthesia management, allowing adjustments according to routine clinical practice at participating centres. This flexibility enhances the generalisability and external validity of the findings, ensuring that the results reflect real-world applicability. Furthermore, the study endpoints extend beyond the primary outcome of PSD incidence to encompass comprehensive evaluation of sleep architecture (N2, N3 stage duration), HADS, QoR-15 and pain levels. This multidimensional assessment, particularly the focus on psychological state, provides a robust dataset to understand the potential clinical benefits of dexmedetomidine via the hypothesised dual-pathway mechanism involving both ‘emotion and sleep’, contributing to a comprehensive understanding of its mode of action. An additional key methodological feature of this study lies in its focus on a homogeneous population undergoing LC. This selection offers significant advantages: LC is a highly standardised surgical procedure, and postoperative pain can be effectively managed via multimodal analgesic regimens, such as the TAP block employed in this study. This homogeneity and controllability of pain create ideal conditions for isolating the major confounding factor of severe pain, thereby enabling a more precise assessment of the direct sleep-promoting effects of dexmedetomidine. Consequently, the significant improvement in sleep quality we observed provides stronger evidence for the independent efficacy of intranasal dexmedetomidine spray in enhancing postoperative sleep. Limitations Concurrently, several limitations deserve mention. Although intraoperative anaesthesia management generally followed the protocol, variations in specific drug choices and management details among centres and anaesthesiologists might have occurred. While this flexibility enhances external validity, it could introduce uncontrolled confounding factors, potentially affecting the precise estimation of dexmedetomidine’s independent effect. The study population is confined to patients undergoing LC, necessitating caution when extrapolating findings to other surgical procedures, especially major operations involving greater physiological stress or longer durations. Moreover, although sleep quality was assessed using subjective scales (AIS, NRS, PSQI) complemented by objective monitoring (wearable devices), the non-application of gold-standard PSG may somewhat limit the depth of analysis regarding sleep architecture changes and their association with emotional improvement. Finally, although the sample size was calculated with an allowance for dropouts, some subgroup analyses might remain underpowered. Nevertheless, through stratified randomisation, rigorous blinding procedures, multicentre participation and standardised assessment tools, we endeavoured to minimise potential biases and enhance findings’ reliability. The results will provide important evidence regarding using intranasal dexmedetomidine for PSD prevention and help lay the groundwork for future interventional studies involving broader patient populations and diverse surgical settings. documents.title: SCCM Surviving Sepsis Campaign international guidelines for management of sepsis and septic shock

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Sepsis is a syndrome that occurs when microorganisms invade and cause systemic disease, which can be life-threatening ( , ). The third international consensus definition of septic shock and sepsis was published in 2016 and defined septic shock as organ dysfunction caused by systemic infection ( ). The immune system is suppressed during sepsis, which leads to increased inflammatory response ( , ). The immune cells are triggered by bacteria, toxins and other factors that result in infection, releasing large quantities of inflammatory mediators ( , ). The release of inflammatory mediators without an appropriate anti-inflammatory response destroys the immune system, resulting in unrestrained inflammatory state and a decreased ability to neutralize pathogens ( – ). Septic cardiomyopathy (SC), or septic shock, is a condition defined by cardiac dysfunction caused by sepsis. SC is clinically characterized by defective left ventricular systolic function and ventricular hypertrophy. According to statistics from the beginning of 2018, up to two-thirds of patients with septic shock experience SC, which has become one of the most common fatal diseases ( ). Therefore, novel pathogenic mechanisms of SC must be researched. The present review aimed to summarize the pathophysiology of SC, focusing on mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic alterations, signaling pathways and other mechanisms. These mechanisms of pathogenesis may be used to validate discovery of novel ways to treat sepsis contribute to decreased mortality in patients with SC. 2. Pathological findings and clinical symptoms Before the onset of SC, pathogenic bacteria that infect the body and their endotoxins enter the bloodstream, stimulating the immune system and producing large amounts of inflammatory factors, leading to cytokine storm ( ). Myocardial dysfunction may be caused by chronic inflammation with prolonged lasting effects. During sepsis, the inflammatory response contributes to an overproduction of catecholamines, which impairs myocardial function and myocardial contractility. Cardiac output is affected when tachycardia leads to reduced coronary perfusion and cardiac output ( ). In addition, mitochondria in septic cardiomyocytes undergo structural changes, DNA damage, elevated permeability and activation of apoptotic pathways, which decrease metabolism, to accommodate inadequate ATP production caused by mitochondrial dysfunction ( ). SC can be characterized by elevated cardiac enzymes, characteristic changes in the electrocardiogram, hemodynamic changes, decreased left ventricular ejection fraction and systolic dysfunction ( ). Clinical treatment is mainly divided into two aspects: Treatment of sepsis characteristics using antibiotics, vasoactive drugs, dopamine, glucocorticoids and antibacterial peptides. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) treats septic cardiomyopathy through anti-inflammatory and anti-viral effects, and inhibition of apoptosis. Currently, TCM injections used clinically include Xuebijing injection and Shenfu injection. 3. Mitochondrial dysfunction ATP is a compound synthesized in mitochondria and the cytosol during glycolysis. Mitochondria are abundant in the heart and are responsible for a significant amount of ATP production ( ). The primary products following substrate oxidation, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide and flavin adenine dinucleotide, provide electrons for complexes I and II. Under physiological conditions, electrons move from complex I to complex II, then from complex III to complex IV by oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) ( ). Complexes I–IV are involved in transferring electrons from the tricarboxylic acid cycle to mitochondria ( ). During this process, a proton can be transferred from the mitochondrial matrix to the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) and O 2 is reduced to H 2 O in the mitochondria ( ). Between the IMM space and the mitochondrial matrix, protons accumulate, causing a proton motive force (ΔΨ). ATP regeneration via F 0 F 1 -ATPase (ATP synthase) is activated by ΔΨ, which transfers the proton from the mitochondrial matrix to the IMM ( – ). Therefore, F 0 F 1 -ATPase activity is associated with respiratory chain activity and ATP formation. In addition, increased superoxide (O 2− ) and nitric oxide (NO) production can cause direct oxidative or nitrosative damage and inhibition of OXPHOS complexes, leading to decreased O 2 consumption and mitochondrial membrane potential. Finally, ΔΨ decreases due to increased uncoupling protein-mediated proton leak and Ca 2+ -induced mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening and direct oxidative damage of the IMM. The mechanism of mitochondrial dysfunction and adaptive response to mitochondrial dysfunction is shown in . Mitochondrial dysfunction is a key component of sepsis ( ). The most commonly used models of sepsis are lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) ( ). In an LPS-induced rat model, the expression of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) γ coactivator 1α (PGC1α) gene, as well as mitochondrial membrane potential, is significantly decreased ( ). Mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes I and II function less efficiently in a CLP-induced rat model ( , ). Reactive oxygen species (ROS) and nitric oxide (NO) Under physiological conditions, mitochondria reduce monovalent O 2 by generating O 2− During substrate oxidation, a small amount of O 2 is reduced by Mn superoxide dismutase to H 2 O 2 . However, a steady state concentration of ROS causes reversible or irreversible modifications to biomolecules, such as protein carbonylation or lipid peroxidation ( , ). In addition, mitochondrial enzymes function normally and mitochondrial DNA is particularly susceptible to damage caused by ROS, leading to incomplete reduction of oxygen and superoxide formation, which leads to ROS production ( ). Decreased production of ROS prevents mitochondrial dysfunction in LPS-induced animal models ( , ). In LPS-induced rat models, increased ROS causes mitochondrial respiratory dysfunction, which leads to septic cardiac disease and performance ( , ). In addition, ROS production is decreased by increasing the activity of complex enzymes in mitochondria in CLP-induced mouse models ( , ). Mitochondria also produce NO via the activity of mitochondrial NO synthase (mtNOS), which physiologically regulates mitochondrial respiration by inhibition of cytochrome C oxidase ( , ). Under physiological conditions, abundant O 2− and NO react to form peroxynitrite (ONOO − ), which acts as a strong oxidizing agent. The enhanced expression of mtNOS is induced in CLP-induced mouse models, which contributes to increased mitochondrial ONOO − levels ( , ). The critical causative factors responsible for mitochondrial dysfunction include inducible NOS (iNOS) synthase and mtNOS. It has been reported that mitochondrial dysfunction is not observed in the iNOS knockout mouse model ( ). Pharmacological inhibition or genetic deletion of iNOS improves heart function in mouse models ( , ). Moreover, studies have found that the activities of complexes I and IV on the IMM are decreased by significantly boosting NO for a long time ( ). Therefore, mitochondrial disorders attributed to NO may be primarily caused by abnormal iNOS expression. At present, most of the aforementioned studies have been conducted on iNOS-induced NO production, which may have some limitations, such as focus only on iNOS induced NO production, with a lack of mtNOS studies. However, NO is produced by multiple NOS isoforms (not only mitochondria) in different intracellular locations and cell types. In summary, one of the major causes of mitochondrial dysfunction involves ROS and NO, which may be key mechanisms of action in sepsis ( ). Calcium transport Mitochondrial membrane permeability occurs within the mitochondrial membrane via the Ca 2+ transport channel mPTP ( ), the primary components of which are ATP synthase dimers and mitochondrial phosphate transporters ( ). The three key processes involved in calcium transport are as follows: Firstly, cyclophilin D activates the pores in response to changes in mitochondrial calcium levels ( ). Secondly, mPTP activation facilitates release of calcium from the mitochondria into the cytosol, where it activates calcium-dependent pathways ( , ). Ca 2+ overload triggers the mPTP to open and release cytochrome C into the cytoplasm and the cytoplasm is released ( ). In addition, the Ca 2+ -dependent state of the mPTP is influenced by the calcium concentration within the cell ( ). Generally, calcium transport causes mitochondrial swelling and dysfunction as a result of calcium transport. A study has shown mitochondrial vacuolation and damaged mitochondrial cristae in cardiomyocytes of septic rats with increased cytochrome C in the cytoplasm ( ). At the same time, the amount of Ca 2+ able to enter the cytoplasm is determined by the number of membrane L-type calcium channels and the amount of Ca 2+ stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum ( ). Additionally, dantrolene prevents mitochondrial Ca 2+ overload, which improves mitochondrial dysfunction, by inhibiting sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca 2+ leaks ( ). Taken together, these conditions may result in cytoplasmic calcium overload, leading to mitochondrial deterioration and contractile dysfunction due to mPTP opening. Drugs for treating mitochondrial dysfunction Triphenylphosphonium (TPP), covalent quinone (MitoQ) and vitamin E have been prescribed as medications for treating SC. A powerful antioxidant targeting mitochondria, MitoQ binds coenzyme Q10 via triphenylphosphine, used for improving mitochondrial function in SC ( ). In a rat model of sepsis, treatment with vitamin E conjugated to TPP decreased ROS-related damage ( ). Additionally, as an antioxidant, lipoic acid might improve mitochondrial performance and alleviate septic shock ( ). To determine whether the treatment modality used to treat mitochondrial dysfunction could be a viable therapeutic option in the future, researchers need to use drugs to prevent or reverse specific mitochondrial functions. 4. Metabolic changes in SC There is evidence that metabolic dysregulation occurs in SC, suggesting that targeting metabolic pathways may offer notable benefits in SC treatment ( ). During sepsis, hypermetabolism is characterized by a catabolic state that depletes carbohydrate, lipid and protein stores ( ). The primary metabolic processes during sepsis involve lipid, ketone, glucose and amino acid metabolism ( ). The physiological indices of lipid metabolism, such as fatty acid oxidation, are reduced during sepsis and the expression of both cardiac fatty acids and lipid metabolizing enzymes is reduced. When glucose is metabolized, glucose oxidation, insulin resistance and cardiac glucose uptake are decreased. Additionally, there is a reduction in the absorption of ketone bodies and amino acids during ketone and amino acid metabolism ( ). Lipid metabolism in SC During sepsis, there is a significant demand for energy, which is met by lipid mobilization ( ). To make up for energy loss, adipose tissue undergoes increased lipolysis to release fatty acid and glycerol into the bloodstream ( ). Sepsis is characterized by notable deregulation of genes typically involved in lipid metabolism due to the inflammatory response, such as PPARα, PGC1α and PPARγ. At the same time, FA metabolism stops when carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1, acyl coenzyme a synthetase and carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 expression is impaired. Studies have shown that LPS reduces PPARα and PGC1α expression in LPS-induced rats, thereby regulating the β-oxidation pathway ( , ). The inhibition of PPARγ activation protects mice from sepsis-related cardiac dysfunction ( ). In addition, studies have found that defects in the enzymes carnitine palmitoyl transferase 1 and CD36 cause inefficient fatty acid transport, which contributes to fatty acid oxidation ( ). Finally, studies have found that LPS reduces enzymes activity related to FA metabolism, such as acyl-CoA synthetase and carnitine palmitoyl transferase-1 ( , ). Imbalance of FA demand and supply between the cytoplasm and mitochondria may cause lipid accumulation in the cytoplasm ( ). Moreover, patients with sepsis exhibit fat buildup in cardiac muscle, kidney and liver ( ). Taken together, lipid metabolism and associated enzyme transport are notable energy providers in sepsis ( ). Ketone metabolism in SC Sepsis may lead to a high metabolic state throughout the body, which increases ketone body production and lipid breakdown ( ). During prolonged fasting, hypoglycemia occurs, resulting in promotion of ketogenesis in hepatocyte mitochondria. The ketogenic effect may serve a valuable role in biodefense as ketone bodies confer resistance to ROS ( ). Ketone body metabolism may increase ATP production or contribute to systemic hypercatabolism associated with calorie restriction ( , ). Ketone metabolism is a method to maintain cardiac energy homeostasis. Studies have found that LPS injection in mice lacking fatty acid binding protein 4 (FABP4) and FABP5 inhibits hepatic and cardiac ketogenesis, as FABP4 serves an active role in FA transport ( , ). At the same time, gene expression associated with 3-oxoacid coenzyme was significantly reduced in both DoubleClick and wild-type mice ( , ). The aforementioned studies suggest that ketone bodies may represent a pathogenic mechanism in sepsis ( ). Glucose metabolism in SC During SC, glucose oxidation does not increase to compensate for the decrease in FAO caused by insulin resistance and glucose metabolism inhibition ( , ). In mice models of endotoxic shock, there is a rapid drop in myocardial glucose levels compared with hemorrhagic shock ( , ) Increased levels of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 2 (PDK2) and PDK4 protein inhibit glucose oxidation ( ). Moreover, 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG) also improves cardiac function and survival outcomes in a mouse model of sepsis ( ). The aforementioned findings indicate that increased glycolytic metabolism contributes to cardiac dysfunction in sepsis and that modulating metabolism following sepsis would be an appropriate strategy ( ). Sepsis activates proteolysis, which splits proteins into smaller polypeptides and amino acids, allowing them to rebuild energy-rich molecules ( – ). It is reported that amino acid uptake by the heart is 90% lower compared with other organs in CLP-induced mouse models ( , ). Moreover, studies have demonstrated that decreases in alanine and

Sepsis activates proteolysis, which splits proteins into smaller polypeptides and amino acids, allowing them to rebuild energy-rich molecules ( – ). Signaling pathway of SC PPAR pathway Nuclear receptor transcription factors regulate metabolic homeostasis, inflammatory response and cell death through nuclear receptors ( , ). Studies have found that PPARα is present in the liver, PPARβ is highly active in skeletal muscle and PPARγ is associated with the control of the inflammatory reaction, apoptosis and sepsis ( , ). PPARγ suppresses expression of pro-inflammatory genes, mainly by scavenging transcription factors and their cofactors, thus preventing binding to their cognate binding sites in the promoters of target genes ( , ). In addition, immune cells can produce large amounts of pro-inflammatory mediators in the early stages of sepsis, and PPARγ regulates sepsis by promoting apoptosis ( , ). In a mouse model of CLP-induced inflammation, inhibition of NF-κB p65 phosphorylation and activation via upregulation of PPARγ attenuates inflammation ( ). Studies have found that total protein concentration, neutrophils and macrophages are reduced in LPS-induced mice ( , ) Decreased inflammatory factor release is attributed to the conversion of macrophages from type M1 to M2. Moreover, the M1 macrophage increases chemokine ligand production in a CLP-induced mouse model by increasing endothelial cell hyperpermeability and phosphorylation of p38 by inhibiting PPARγ ( ). In conclusion, activation of PPARγ may contribute to reduction of pro-inflammatory properties during SC ( ). NF-κB pathway The predominant form of NF-κB is a heterodimer of p50 and p65 proteins ( ). The protein is normally sequestered in the cytosol by a class of inhibitory proteins known as IκBs. These comprise seven members, including IκBα, IκBβ and IκΒγ ( ). Under physiological conditions, NF-κB forms a complex with IκBα to undergo cytoplasmic sequestration. When stimulated by activating signals, NF-κB undergoes phosphorylation, ubiquitination and degradation, which leads to an activated NF-κB form that travels to the nucleus to induce gene transcription ( ). NF-κB attenuates sepsis-induced systemic inflammation and myocardial injury by inhibiting NF-κB signaling ( ). Additionally, studies have demonstrated that suppressing NF-κB activation decreases systemic hypotension, improves septic myocardial dysfunction and vascular abnormality, inhibits expression of numerous pro-inflammatory genes, decreases intravascular coagulation and neutrophil infiltration and prevents endothelial leakage ( , ). When the NF-κB signaling pathway is engaged, phosphorylation of NF-κB pathway factors such as p65 and inhibitor κBα occurs ( , ). Moreover, studies have shown that decreasing TNF-α and IL-6 secretion, cytokines that promote inflammation in a LPS-induced rat model, stimulates the NF-κB signaling pathway ( , ). In summary, NF-κB suppresses inflammatory factors and proinflammatory genes that might be involved in sepsis symptoms ( ). 6. Association between cell death and SC Association between ferroptosis and SC Ferroptosis pathways are iron-dependent, non-apoptotic and characterized by specific biochemical and morphological changes ( ). The majority of iron in the body is bound to hemoglobin and myoglobin, with the rest primarily bound to ferritin and transferrin ( ). In some cases, the cellular defense mechanism limits the cell iron export system, leading to an overload of cellular iron. Peroxylated lipids are produced as a result of the Fenton reaction, resulting in the damage of organelles ( ). The bloodstream contains tetrapyrrole hemoglobin containing iron during SC. Under the action of heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1) enzyme, stable heme is degraded to biliverdin, carbon monoxide and iron in vivo ( , ). Additionally, HO-1 induces immunosuppression during sepsis, promotes helper T cell 1(Th1) to Th2 cytokine transfer and induces apoptosis in immune cells ( ). The product of the HO-1 reaction is unstable iron, which promotes synthesis of ferritin and reduces the toxic effects of iron. The abnormal activation of HO-1 may result in the loss of the antioxidant action, increase levels of the labile iron pool (LIP) and eventually cause iron deficiency ( ). In a mouse model of sepsis, the expression of HO-1 leads to altered iron metabolism protein levels and ferroptosis ( ). Taken together, HO-1 causes ferroptosis by degrading heme and elevating LIP to release ferritin into the body. Hepcidin, a liver-derived peptide hormone, maintains iron homeostasis in the body. Association between pyroptosis and SC Under physiological conditions, pyroptosis is mediated by inflammasome-activated caspases and gasdermin D (GSDMD), final effectors of the GSDM protein family, leading to pore formation in the plasma membrane and leakage of inflammatory mediators ( , ). Under pathogenic conditions, LPS from Gram-negative bacteria directly activates caspase 4/5/11, in the inflammasome pathway, without the need for the inflammasome or caspase-1. GSDMD can be cleaved to produce N-GSDMD by activated caspase 4/5/11. N-GSDMD indirectly promotes NLRP3 inflammasome assembly via K + efflux, which aggravates pyroptosis ( , ). Studies have found that doxorubicin upregulates NADPH oxidase 1 and NADPH oxidase 4 expression, thereby activating dynamin-related protein-1and promoting mitochondrial fission, leading to excessive accumulation of ROS in mitochondria and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and caspase-1dependent apoptosis ( , ) Certain studies have found that GSDMD knockout significantly decreases NLRP3 and caspase-1 expression, increases survival and improves cardiac dysfunction in mice ( , ). Moreover, LPS directly affects nuclear localization of sting and interferon regulatory factor-3-activated sting then activates NLRP3, leading to cardiac dysfunction as well as pyroptosis ( ). Collectively, pyroptosis is induced in most forms of cardiomyopathy and blocking pyroptosis by direct or indirect approaches that target the pyroptotic machinery or upstream regulators may exert a protective effect. 7. Conclusion and future research prospects Myocardial dysfunction caused by sepsis is one of the main reasons for the high mortality rate of sepsis and it is crucial to investigate the pathogenesis of sepsis-induced cardiac dysfunction and find treatment methods. The present study summarized the primary factors that contribute to the pathogenesis of SC, such as mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic changes, cell death and signaling pathways. Mitochondrial dysfunction, primarily due to increased ROS and no steady-state concentrations inside mitochondria, increases various reversible and irreversible toxic modifications on biomolecules, such as protein carbonylation and lipid peroxidation ( , ). Meanwhile, excessive ROS and NO damage the mitochondrial respiratory chain structure and aggravate the biosynthesis of ROS ( , ). Metabolism in sepsis requires the adjustment of immune function via metabolism of fat, the metabolism of amino acids, metabolism of glucose and the absorption of a large amount of energy from cell's own metabolism ( , ). In addition, ferroptosis and pyroptosis contribute to pathogenesis of SC. Iron molecules contribute to the aggregation of ferritin at the cell membrane through the HO-1 reaction; however, activation of iron molecules by ferritin leads to an increase in iron output, leading to iron enrichment ( , ). By regulating the key molecule GSDMD, pyroptosis activates NLRP 3 inflammatory bodies and caspase 1-dependent apoptosis, leading to myocardial dysfunction in sepsis ( , ). According to previous treatment methods, the relevant methods for the treatment of sepsis were divided into two main categories, the first category was the basic treatment methods for the characteristics of sepsis. Antibiotics decrease the release of inflammatory factors and mediators by regulating pathogenic microorganisms and the immune system to improve shock relieve clinical symptoms and signs of sepsis ( , ). Dopamine, a vasoactive drug, maintains a steady state of cardiac function by regulating the mean arterial tone ( , ). Glucocorticoids are effective in decreasing the duration of vasopressor use and maintaining haemodynamic balance and improve the clinical symptoms of patients with sepsis within a short period of time ( , ). The second type of treatment is herbal injections, whose mechanism of action is to attenuate the release of inflammatory factors and increase body immunity. Effective interventions to control the way sepsis develops are necessary to translate basic research into clinical practice. Knowledge of sepsis and heart failure may lead to better treatment of myocardial infarction in future. To the best of our knowledge, the metabolism of cells has not been investigated in SC. Secondly, although metabolic changes during sepsis have been reported, there is a lack of information on specific mechanism of action studies. Lastly, it is unclear how ferroptosis and pyroptosis occur during SC. Therefore, researchers should investigate the pathogenesis of SC using new methods and tools, such as network pharmacology, proteomics, metabolomics and gut microbiota analysis. The present study reviewed the pathogenesis of SC with the goal of providing new ideas for the prevention and treatment of SC. In conclusion, this review summarizes the mitochondrial dysfunction (including reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide and calcium ion transport), metabolic changes (including lipid metabolism, ketone body metabolism, glucose metabolism and amino acid metabolism) and cell death modes (including iron death and cellular pyroptosis) associated with septic cardiomyopathy during sepsis. SC was not caused by all pathogenic mechanisms, but only a few that were relatively important were discussed in the review.
